q: What is Scrum?
options: A scaling framework for many teams
A project scheduling tool
A single-team process framework for managing product development in sprints
A type of contract
explanation: Scrum is a single-team process framework consisting of roles, events, artifacts and rules, using an iterative approach to deliver working products.

q: How long is a sprint?
options: One month or less, with a consistent length
Exactly one week
Any length that the customer chooses each time
Three to six months
explanation: Scrum runs on timeboxes of one month or less with consistent durations, called sprints, each producing a potentially releasable increment.

q: Which are the three roles in a Scrum team?
options: Project manager, sponsor, team member
Scrum master, project manager, tester
Product owner, business analyst, lead developer
Product owner, development team, scrum master
explanation: The Scrum team consists of a product owner, a development team and a scrum master. Scrum has no project manager role.

q: A Scrum team has far more requests than it can ever build. Someone must decide what is most valuable and keep the product backlog in order. Who is responsible for that?
options: The scrum master
The product owner
The development team
The sponsor
explanation: The product owner is responsible for maximizing the value of the product and ranks the work based on its business value.

q: Which statement best describes the scrum master?
options: The manager who assigns tasks to team members
The person who decides which features to build
A servant leader who upholds the Scrum process, coaches the team and removes impediments
The customer's representative
explanation: The scrum master helps ensure the Scrum process is followed and coaches the team on removing impediments. The role is a supportive leader, not a boss.

q: What does it mean that the development team is cross-functional?
options: It has all the skills needed to deliver the working product without depending on people outside the team
Each member belongs to several teams
It reports to several managers
It works in different time zones
explanation: A cross-functional team has everything it needs within the team to deliver the working product, so it can finish work quickly without external dependencies.

q: In sprint planning the product owner presents twelve stories and says she needs all of them this sprint. Who decides how much work the team will take into the sprint?
options: The product owner
The scrum master
The project's sponsor
The development team
explanation: The team considers its capacity and story size so that it does not commit to more than it can complete in one iteration. The product owner sets priorities; the team decides how much fits.

q: Which of the following is a Scrum artifact?
options: Sprint review
Sprint backlog
Daily scrum meeting
Scrum master
explanation: The three Scrum artifacts are the product backlog, the sprint backlog and the increment. The sprint review and daily scrum are events.

q: What is the product backlog?
options: The list of defects found in testing
The work the team selected for the current sprint
The ordered list of all the work for the product
The team's improvement actions
explanation: The backlog is the ordered list of all the work for a team. It does not need to be complete before work starts and changes as more is learned.

q: A daily scrum has been running for 40 minutes, because two developers are solving a design problem in front of everyone. What is the maximum length of the daily scrum?
options: 15 minutes
30 minutes
1 hour
As long as needed to solve the problems raised
explanation: The daily coordination meeting is timeboxed to no longer than 15 minutes.

q: During the daily scrum, two developers start a detailed discussion about how to fix a technical problem. What should happen?
options: Extend the meeting for as long as it takes, until the whole team has solved the problem
Cancel the sprint
Ask the product owner to decide
Note the problem in a parking lot and let those involved solve it after the meeting
explanation: Daily coordination meetings are for realizing there are problems, not for solving them. Issues go to a parking lot and are handled in a separate discussion.

q: Each morning a team holds its daily scrum around the manager's desk, and the members take turns telling the manager what they did yesterday. Which common mistake with the daily scrum is this?
options: Keeping it to 15 minutes
Turning it into a status report to a manager
Letting any member of the team facilitate it each day
Reviewing the task board
explanation: A typical antipattern is that the daily meeting becomes a status meeting. It exists for the team to self-organize and make commitments to one another.

q: What is the purpose of the sprint review?
options: To improve the team's way of working
To plan the next sprint in detail and estimate each of the selected stories
To demonstrate the working increment to stakeholders and get feedback
To assign tasks for the day
explanation: The team demonstrates completed work at the end of the iteration. The product owner accepts or declines stories and feedback shapes what comes next.

q: What is the purpose of the sprint retrospective?
options: For the team to learn from its work and improve its process
To show the product to the customer
To decide who is to blame for defects
To update the product roadmap and the release plan for stakeholders
explanation: The retrospective allows the team to learn about, improve and adapt its process. It is not about blame.

q: A retrospective produces 14 possible improvements. What should the team do?
options: Start all 14 in the next sprint
Ignore them, because the sprint is already planned
Give all of them to the scrum master to implement alone before the next sprint
Rank them and choose a small number the team has capacity to complete
explanation: The team should limit the action items to its capacity. Trying to improve too many things and finishing none is worse than completing a few.

q: At the demonstration the team shows five completed stories. One of them does not behave as the customer expected. Who accepts or declines the completed stories?
options: The scrum master
The product owner
The development team
The project sponsor
explanation: The product owner sees the demonstration and accepts or declines stories.

q: A scrum team wants one shared way to decide whether an increment is really finished. Which of these is its definition of done?
options: The date the sprint ends
The list of items in the sprint backlog
The team's shared checklist of what an increment must meet to be considered finished
The product owner's vision for the product
explanation: A clear definition of done gives the team a shared view of what ready to ship means: integrated, tested, compliant, documented and accepted.

q: At the end of a sprint, one story is coded but not yet tested, so it does not meet the definition of done. What should happen?
options: It is not counted as done and returns to the product backlog to be re-prioritized
It is demonstrated as complete
The sprint is extended by a few days
The definition of done is relaxed for this sprint so that the story can be counted
explanation: Work that does not meet the definition of done is not done. The sprint length is fixed, so the item goes back to the backlog.
ref: The Scrum Guide, Commitment: Definition of Done; Agile Practice Guide, 5.2.8

q: In the middle of a sprint, a stakeholder asks a developer to add an urgent new feature. What should the developer do?
options: Add it to the sprint immediately
Refuse and ignore the request
Ask the scrum master to approve it
Direct the stakeholder to the product owner, who can add it to the product backlog and prioritize it
explanation: The product owner owns the backlog and its order. New requests go to the product owner, so the team can stay focused on the sprint's work.
ref: The Scrum Guide, The Sprint; Agile Practice Guide, 4.4.2

q: When does backlog refinement usually take place, and what is it for?
options: At the end of the project, to archive the backlog
During the sprint, to prepare and clarify stories for upcoming sprints
Only before the first sprint, to write every story in full detail up front
During the retrospective, to assign blame
explanation: Refinement sessions are typically held in the middle of an iteration to get stories ready for upcoming iterations, so the team understands them and their relative size.

q: Which three questions are answered in the daily scrum?
options: Who is late, who is absent, who is on leave
What the budget is, what the schedule is, what the scope is, and who approved them
What I completed, what I plan to complete next, what my impediments are
What went well, what went badly, what to improve
explanation: Each person says what they completed since the last meeting, what they plan to complete before the next one and what impediments they have.

q: Which statement about the sprint review and the retrospective is correct?
options: The review inspects the product with stakeholders; the retrospective inspects the process within the team
Both are attended only by the scrum master
The retrospective comes before the review
They are two names for the same meeting
explanation: The review demonstrates the working product and gathers feedback. The retrospective, the last event of the sprint, is where the team improves its way of working.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, 5.2.6; Agile Practice Guide, 5.2.7

q: A team that works without iterations holds its standup in front of its kanban board, reading the columns from right to left. According to the 2017 Agile Practice Guide, which question does a flow-based team ask?
options: What did I complete since the last standup?
How many story points did each person finish yesterday?
What do we need to do to advance this piece of work?
Which stories should go into the next sprint?
explanation: Flow-based teams focus on throughput and assess the board from right to left, asking what is needed to advance each piece of work, whether anyone is working on something not on the board, what the team needs to finish, and whether there are bottlenecks.

q: A team finds it is spending four hours every week refining stories for the next batch of work. According to the 2017 Agile Practice Guide, what might this show?
options: The product owner may be overpreparing, or the team may lack skills it needs
The team is working exactly as an agile team should
The iterations are too short and should be made longer
The scrum master should refine the stories alone, so the team can keep building
explanation: Teams often aim to spend no more than one hour a week refining stories, to maximize time spent doing the work. Needing more can mean the product owner is overpreparing or the team lacks critical skills to evaluate and refine the work.

q: The scrum master is away for a week, and the team wonders whether the daily standup can go ahead. What does the 2017 Agile Practice Guide say?
options: It must wait, since only the scrum master may run it
The product owner has to take it over
The functional manager should run it meanwhile
Anyone from the team can facilitate it
explanation: The team runs its own standup, and anyone from the team can facilitate it. The guide encourages this, so that the standup does not turn into a status meeting for a leader.

q: A new product owner wants to write every story for the whole project before the team starts its first iteration. What does the 2017 Agile Practice Guide advise?
options: Write them all in detail, so that the scope of the project is fixed before any work begins
Write enough to understand the first release broadly, and enough items for the next iteration
Write none in advance, and decide the work each morning
Write only the stories the developers ask her to write
explanation: There is no need to create all the stories for the entire project before work starts: only enough to understand the first release in broad brushstrokes, and then sufficient items for the next iteration.

q: A team that works in continuous flow has no fixed refinement meeting. When a slot opens, it takes the next card from the to-do column and discusses it there and then. What does the 2017 Agile Practice Guide call this?
options: Sprint planning
Just-in-time refinement
A timeboxed refinement hour for the team
A retrospective
explanation: The guide describes a continuum: just-in-time refinement for flow-based agile, where the team takes the next card off the to-do column and discusses it; a timeboxed one-hour discussion midway through a two-week iteration; or several refinement discussions for teams new to the product.

q: A product owner drew a product roadmap at the start of the year. After four iterations the team has delivered less of one feature set and more of another than the roadmap showed. What does the 2017 Agile Practice Guide say she does with the roadmap?
options: Keeps it unchanged, since it is a commitment
Hands it over to the scrum master to maintain from then on
Discards it, since agile teams do not use roadmaps
Replans it, based on what the team produces
explanation: Product owners may produce a product roadmap to show the anticipated sequence of deliverables over time. The product owner replans the roadmap based on what the team produces.

q: Match each purpose with the Scrum event.
left: Decide what will be delivered this sprint, and how
Show the increment to stakeholders and get feedback
explanation: Sprint planning opens the sprint. The daily scrum coordinates the day. The sprint review looks at the product with stakeholders; the sprint retrospective looks at how the team works.

q: Match each Scrum artifact with who owns it.
explanation: The product owner owns the ordered list of all the work for the product. The development team owns the items it selected for the sprint and its plan for delivering them. The increment belongs to the whole Scrum team.

q: Which event will the stakeholder attend?

strip.says: When can I see what the team built this sprint, and say what I think of it?
At the end of the sprint. The team shows the increment and collects your feedback.
And the meeting about how the team works together?
That is a different event, for the Scrum team.

options: Sprint planning
The daily scrum
The sprint review
The sprint retrospective
explanation: The sprint review shows the increment to stakeholders and gathers feedback. The sprint retrospective is where the Scrum team improves how it works.
